newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Fuji Photo denies price war with Kodak.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Fuji Photo denies price war with Kodak.

text.p: Major Japanese photographic film maker Fuji Photo Film Co Ltd says it is not engaged in a price war with its biggest rival Eastman Kodak Co in the U.S. photo film market.
"We have not cut prices," Fuji Photo managing director Tasuku Imai told Reuters in a recent interview.
"At least, I believe that we have not been engaging in a price competition (with Kodak). It is our policy...to try to expand sales through improved quality and services," Imai said.

Concerns that Kodak is facing pressure over prices from Fuji Photo in the United States have recently dampened Kodak's shares. A Prudential Securities analyst said Kodak may have lost three to four percent of its share of the market for 35 mm film in the United States so far this year to Fuji Photo.

Kodak and Fuji Photo are already locked in a dispute over access to Japan's photographic film market, which the U.S. government has said was a trade spat between two countries and not a fight between the two firms.

Earlier this year, the United States filed a complaint with the World Trade Organisation (WTO) alleging that Japan for the last 30 years has imposed laws, regulations and other administrative steps to strengthen its domestic industry and curtail opportunities for foreign firms.
The WTO is not expected to reach a decision on the dispute until October.

In terms of its overseas business, Imai said Fuji Photo has plans to strengthen operations at its factory in Boston, which makes recording devices, but the investment in the plant would not be a major one.
Fuji Photo has put a high priority on its recording device business, which will grow further in the future, Imai said.

As for investment in other markets, Imai said China was viewed as a potentially huge market and that Fuji Photo would continue to strengthen its production there, although the value of investment in China might not be large.
Fuji Photo has no immediate plans to take out fresh bank loans for investment purposes, but its overseas units may issue commercial paper abroad, Imai said.
Last year, Fuji Photo bought six of U.S. retailer Wal-Mart Stores Inc's laboratories, strengthening its presence in the United States.
Imai said the acquisition would help push up Fuji Photo's group sales in the current 1997/98 business year.

Fuji Photo's sales volume so far this business year has been in line with the business projections it announced in May, but its profits may differ from the outlook, depending on the dollar/yen exchange rate, Imai said.
A rise in the yen of one yen against the dollar, for example, trims Fuji Photo's annual sales by 1.5 billion yen ($13.2 million) and profits by 1.2 billion yen ($10.6 million), he said.

He said that the firm would review early next month the estimates made in May, when it saw a group net profit of 89 billion yen ($787 million) for 1997/98 based on U.S. accounting rules, up 4.3 percent from the year before. It forecast group sales of 1.36 trillion yen ($12.0 billion) for the year, up from 1.25 trillion yen ($11.0 billion) in 1996/97.
The May forecast was based on an assumption that the dollar would average 117 yen for the year. The dollar stood at around 113.70 yen late on Wednesday.
Imai said, however, that 1997/98 profits will be hurt by a year-on-year rise in depreciation costs of 4.2 billion yen ($37.1 million).

In order to fend off the various negative factors on profits, Fuji Photo is trying to cut production and domestic labour costs. It aims to cut its work force to 10,000 by the end of March 1998, from 10,717 as of March 31, 1997, he said. ($1=113 yen)
